newsitem.title: USA: Minn. top lawyer warns against hasty tobacco pact.
newsitem.headline: Minn. top lawyer warns against hasty tobacco pact.

text.p: With tobacco talks set to resume next week, Minnesota's attorney general asked colleagues Friday whether it was the right time to settle with cigarette makers, saying they may be able to bring the industry "to its knees."
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey, who has taken a hard line against settlement with the tobacco industry, wrote to officials from other states and warned them against a hasty accord.
"Is this the right time to settle?" Humphrey asked in his letter to the other attorneys general.
"Frankly, it may not be. We have strong cases and if we try and win even a few, we will have brought the industry not just to the table, but to its knees," he said.

Representatives from the major tobacco makers began talks with the attorneys general early last month in an effort to resolve mounting litigation against the industry and they are expected to resume negotiations as soon as Monday.

"I have repeatedly asked for a more deliberative process with a realistic timetable and questioned the need to rush to judgment on such fundamental questions involving the nation's No. 1 public health issue," Humphrey said in his letter.
A total of 24 attorneys general have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers. Mississippi's suit is set to be the first of these cases to go to trial in July.

The negotiations have been criticised by health groups, some congressmen and plaintiffs' lawyers who worry that an accord would not adequately address concerns about regulation of cigarette sales and advertising and youth smoking.
They have also urged that the industry should not receive total immunity from lawsuits.

Indeed, a session was being held in Chicago Friday to explain negotiations to such high-profile organisations as the American Cancer Society, the American Heart Association, and the American Medical Association, among others.

Scepticism about the talks led a number of attorneys general, who attended a strategy meeting on Monday, to tell reporters that they were united in their opposition to any proposal that would provide total immunity to manufacturers.
While the state lawyers presented a unified front on the immunity issue, Humphrey's letter expressed scepticism about the talks and he emphasised that no one had the power to negotiate for him.

"I have not authorised anyone to make proposals on behalf of or to settle Minnesota's litigation. And any settlement must resolve the public health, law enforcement and victims' rights issues which lie at the heart of our efforts," he said.

His letter raised other questions he felt his colleagues should consider. Among them was whether an accord would preserve "full" Food and Drug Administration jurisdiction over tobacco products and content, including nicotine.
Last week a federal judge ruled that the FDA had the authority to regulate the sale and labeling of cigarettes, but not advertising.

Humphrey also said the negotiators should consider what an accord would do to help the nation's 50 million addicted tobacco users and others affected by second-hand smoke, and whether a settlement would provide an incentive for manufacturers to develop less dangerous products.
He also raised concerns about whether the creation of a fund to pay for injuries would pre-empt individual and state suits and how much money would be adequate to cover damages.
